relevance_reason: Identifies intronic ATTTC repeat expansions in STARD7 as the cause of chr2-linked FAME2, segregating in 158 affected individuals from 22 families.

findings.statement: Corbett et al. (2019) described FAME as characterized by cortical myoclonic tremor and overt myoclonic and later generalized tonic-clonic seizures, with onset in the second to third decade, variable expressivity within and between families, and anticipation in some families. Seizures are typically controlled with antiepileptic drugs for generalized epilepsies, although drug resistance occurs rarely.
quotes: FAME (also referred to as Familial Cortical Myoclonic Tremor and Epilepsy or Benign Adult onset Familial Myoclonic Epilepsy [OMIM phenotypic series: PS601068]) is characterised by cortical myoclonic tremor and overt myoclonic and later generalised tonic-clonic seizures (GTCS).
Onset of symptoms occurs in the second to third decade with variable expressivity within and between families; anticipation has been noted in some families.
Seizures are typically controlled with anti-epileptic drugs for generalised epilepsies, although rarely individuals have drug resistant epilepsy.

findings.statement: Corbett et al. (2019) summarized clinical data on 22 FAME2 families (Australian/New Zealand, Italian, Iraqi and Israeli of Sephardic Jewish ancestry, South African, French/Spanish, French, and Syrian). Myoclonus/cortical tremor was present in nearly all affected individuals, whereas the frequency of tonic-clonic seizures varied from 15 to 100% between families; focal seizures occurred in a minority. In the large Australian/New Zealand family (family 1), 55 individuals were affected with mean onset 18.6 years (range 4-59), all had myoclonus/cortical tremor, 8/55 had tonic-clonic seizures, and 2/55 had focal seizures.
quotes: The frequency of GTCS varies from 15 to 100% in 22 different families reported here (Table 1).
1 | Australian/New Zealand of European ancestry | 55 | 18.6 y [4–59,60 y] | 55/55 (100%) | 8/55 (15%) | 2/55 (4%) |
findings.population: Australian/New Zealand; Italian; Sephardic Jewish; South African; French/Spanish; Syrian

findings.statement: In affected members of 3 FAME2 families (Australian/New Zealand, Italian, French/Spanish), Corbett et al. (2019) used whole-genome sequencing with repeat-expansion detection (ExpansionHunter and exSTRa) to identify an expansion of an ATTTT repeat with insertion of an ATTTC repeat in intron 1 of STARD7. The ATTTC repeat was absent from 69 control genomes. By repeat-primed PCR, the ATTTC expansion was found in 137/137 affected individuals from 16 previously reported FAME2 families and in 20/20 familial cases from 6 further families and 1 of 52 unrelated singletons, for a total of 158 affected individuals from 22 families; 2 of 24 unaffected relatives tested positive, both from younger generations and likely presymptomatic. The expansion was not amplified in 28 control DNA samples.
quotes: This revealed an expansion of an ATTTT repeat and insertion of an ATTTC repeat in the context of the reverse strand of chr2 within the first intron of STARD7 (StAR-related lipid transfer domain-containing 7) in all FAME samples tested
We developed a repeat-primed PCR (RP-PCR) assay to rapidly identify the expansion in 137/137 affected individuals from 16 independently reported FAME2 families worldwide
Of these, 20/20 familial and 1/52 singleton cases were positive for an ATTTC expansion in STARD7

variants.as_reported: intronic ATTTC repeat insertion/expansion with ATTTT expansion, intron 1

findings.statement: Corbett et al. (2019) used long-read sequencing to characterize the repeat structure as (AAATG)n[N](AAAAT)n on the forward strand. In one patient from family 1, a PacBio read contained 274 AAATG and 387 AAAAT repeats and a nanopore read contained 345 AAATG and 390 AAAAT repeats, suggesting somatic variability; in a patient from family 5, a read showed 588 AAATG and 340 AAAAT repeats (4,645 bp). The endogenous ATTTT repeat was variable in length in the normal population.
quotes: This suggested the structure of the pathogenic repeat in the context of the forward strand of chr2 was (AAATG)n[N](AAAAT)n, where (n) represents the unknown number of each repeat sequence.
The Oxford Nanopore read contained 345 AAATG and 390 AAAAT repeats with some interruptions, suggesting somatic variation of repeat sizes may occur within the one individual.
In a second individual (Family 5; III-37), a single Oxford Nanopore read spanned the expanded repeats with 588 AAATG and 340 AAAAT repeats; 4645 bp in total length.

findings.statement: Corbett et al. (2019) found the STARD7 ATTTC repeat in 2 families carrying the previously proposed ADRA2B variant (c.675_686delTGGTGGGGCTTTinsGTTTGGCAG), strongly suggesting that the ADRA2B allele is not causative.
quotes: This included two families with the previously identified ADRA2B; c.675_686delTGGTGGGGCTTTinsGTTTGGCAG; p.H225_L229delinsQ225_F_G_R228 variant strongly suggesting that allele is not causative (Table 1; Family 4 & 15).

findings.statement: Corbett et al. (2019) found evidence of anticipation in the large Australian/New Zealand FAME2 family: median onset was 30 years in generation III, 17 years in generation IV, and 12 years in generation V.
quotes: We found evidence of anticipation; generation III had a median onset of 30 years (range 14–60 y, n = 6), in generation IV median onset was 17 years (8–50 y, n = 30) and the median onset in generation V was 12 years (4–19 y, n = 16).

findings.statement: Corbett et al. (2019) found no change in STARD7 mRNA (qPCR, RNA-seq) or protein levels (Western blot) in patient-derived fibroblasts, and no reads containing ATTTC repeats in RNA-seq data. They suggested that the repeat sequence alone is pathogenic, independent of an effect on the encompassing gene, possibly via RNA toxicity as proposed for other ATTTC expansion disorders.
quotes: Reads containing ATTTC repeats were not present in the RNA-Seq data despite robust expression of STARD7.
These data suggest the repeat sequence alone is pathogenic, independent of an effect on the coding sequence of the encompassing gene.
Protein abundance was also unaltered, confirmed by western blotting using an antibody to STARD7 protein that was previously validated using STARD7-knockout cell lines (Fig. 3b).

findings.statement: Corbett et al. (2019) reported that the ATTTC repeat-primed PCR assay was diagnostic for FAME with 100% sensitivity in all families with linkage or suggestive linkage to chromosome 2, and noted that FAME2 is the most frequently observed linked locus in Caucasian patients.
quotes: the ATTTC repeat primer was diagnostic for FAME with a sensitivity of 100% in all families with linkage or suggestive linkage to chr2.
The FAME2 locus is the most frequently observed linked region for Caucasian individuals affected by this disorder whereas chromosome 8 thus far is limited to Asian individuals

relevance_reason: Natural history study of 14 patients from 3 families linked to 2p11.1-q12.2 (the FAME2 locus).

findings.statement: Coppola et al. (2011) evaluated the clinical, electrophysiologic, and treatment data of 14 patients from 3 families with autosomal dominant cortical tremor, myoclonus, and epilepsy linked to chromosome 2p11.1-q12.2. Mean age at onset was 20.2 years (range 11 to 40 years), and mean follow-up was 14.0 years. Myoclonus worsened gradually in 10 patients (71.4%), and severity correlated with disease duration and patient age. Two patients older than 80 years had myoclonus that interfered with walking on their own. Six patients (42.8%) had seizures, usually between the second and sixth decades of life, and more than a third had psychiatric and neuropsychological dysfunction.
quotes: We evaluated the clinical, electrophysiologic, and treatment data of 14 patients from three families linked to 2p11.1-q12.2.

Mean age at disease onset was 20.2 ± 7.8 years (range 11-40 years); mean follow-up duration was 14.0 ± 5.8 years (range 7-28 years). Evaluation at different age groups revealed a gradual, progressive worsening of the myoclonus in 10 patients (71.4%).
Six patients (42.8%) experienced seizures, usually between the second and sixth decades of life.

findings.statement: Coppola et al. (2011) found that, over the long term, EEG background activity slowed progressively as the myoclonus worsened. In contrast, paroxysmal activity and photosensitivity were most evident in the intermediate phases of the disease. The authors concluded that the disorder shows slight age-dependent progression. They suggested that the name 'familial or autosomal dominant cortical tremor, myoclonus, and epilepsy' (FCTME/ADCME) was more appropriate.
quotes: Evaluation of EEG long-term evolution revealed progressive slowing of background activity in parallel with the gradual worsening of myoclonus. In contrast, paroxysmal activity and photosensitivity were particularly evident during the intermediate phases of the disease.

We provide data for a slight age-dependent progression and the presence of neuropsychiatric and neuropsychological dysfunction in this unique syndrome, for which the definition of familial or autosomal dominant cortical tremor, myoclonus, and epilepsy (FCTME/ADCME) seems to be, therefore, more appropriate.

relevance_reason: This paper describes the original ADCME (FAME2) pedigree, giving its clinical and neurophysiologic features and mapping the disorder to 2p11.1-q12.2.

findings.statement: Guerrini et al. (2001) described a pedigree with 8 affected individuals who had a non-progressive disorder beginning between ages 12 and 50 years. All patients had predominantly distal, semi-continuous rhythmic myoclonus and generalized tonic-clonic seizures, and 3 had complex partial seizures. Most rarely had seizures and had normal cognition, but 3 with intractable seizures had mild mental retardation. The authors named the disorder autosomal dominant cortical myoclonus and epilepsy (ADCME).
quotes: We describe a pedigree in which eight individuals presented with a non-progressive disorder with onset between the ages of 12 and 50 years.
It was characterized by predominantly distal, semi-continuous rhythmic myoclonus (all patients), generalized tonic-clonic seizures (all patients) and complex partial seizures (three patients).
Most individuals had rarely suffered seizures and had a normal cognitive level, but three individuals with intractable seizures had mild mental retardation.

phenotypes.hpo_label: Bilateral tonic-clonic seizure with generalized onset

findings.statement: Guerrini et al. (2001) found that all affected members of the ADCME pedigree had frontotemporal as well as generalized interictal EEG abnormalities. Neurophysiologic studies suggested a cortical origin for the myoclonus: back-averaging showed EEG waves whose frequency matched the EMG bursts. In 5 patients, EMG and EEG over the contralateral rolandic area showed significant coherence at 8 to 25 Hz, with EEG activity preceding EMG activity by 8 to 15 ms. In 2 individuals, ipsilateral EEG–EMG coherence was consistent with transcallosal spread of myoclonic activity.
quotes: All patients had frontotemporal as well as generalized interictal EEG abnormalities. A neurophysiological study of the myoclonus suggested a cortical origin.

Frequency analysis identified significant peaks with coherence between EMG and EEG, which were recorded over the contralateral rolandic area in five patients. The frequency of coherence was 8-25 Hz and phase spectra confirmed that EEG activity preceded EMG activity by 8-15 ms.
In two individuals there was also significant coherence between the ipsilateral EEG and EMG, consistent with the transcallosal spread of myoclonic activity.

findings.statement: Guerrini et al. (2001) found an enhanced C-reflex at rest and high-amplitude somatosensory and visual evoked potentials in patients with ADCME. Compared with controls, patients had a significantly reduced resting motor threshold to transcranial magnetic stimulation (38%) and a significantly shorter post-motor evoked potential silent period (101 ms vs 137 ms in controls). The authors suggested that these findings reflect diffuse cortical hyperexcitability that particularly involves frontotemporal circuits.
quotes: The C-reflex at rest was enhanced and somatosensory and visual evoked potentials were of high amplitude.

The resting motor threshold intensity to transcranial magnetic stimulation was significantly reduced (38%; SD +/- 7; P = 0.01) and the post-motor evoked potential silent period (101 ms; SEM +/- 10) was significantly shortened compared with the controls (137 ms; SEM +/- 18).
We hypothesize that the responsible gene causes cortical hyperexcitability that is widespread but particularly involves the frontotemporal circuits.

findings.statement: Guerrini et al. (2001) found that ADCME was inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern with high penetrance in the family they studied.
quotes: The pattern of inheritance was autosomal dominant with high penetrance.

findings.statement: In a genome-wide linkage analysis of the ADCME family, Guerrini et al. (2001) identified a 12.4-cM critical region on 2p11.1-q12.2 between markers D2S2161 and D2S1897. The maximum 2-point lod score was 3.46 at theta = 0.0 for marker D2S2175, and the multipoint lod score reached 3.74 around D2S2175.
quotes: Genome-wide linkage analysis identified a critical region spanning 12.4 cM between markers D2S2161 and D2S1897 in 2p11.1-q12.2, with a maximum two-point LOD score of 3.46 at Theta 0.0 for marker D2S2175.
Multipoint LOD score values, reaching 3.74 around D2S2175, localize the ADCME gene to the centromeric region of chromosome 2.

findings.statement: Guerrini et al. (2001) excluded linkage of their family to the familial adult myoclonic epilepsy locus on chromosome 8q23.3-q24. Together with the new localization to 2cen and the different phenotype, the authors concluded that ADCME is a new epilepsy syndrome.
quotes: The exclusion of the locus for familial adult myoclonic epilepsy on chromosome 8q23.3-q24 from linkage to our family and the new localization of the responsible gene to chromosome 2cen, together with the different phenotype, define a new epilepsy syndrome.

relevance_reason: The title reports refining the 2p11.1-q12.2 locus for cortical tremor associated with epilepsy (FAME2) and excluding candidate genes. Only the title was available.

findings.statement: Saint-Martin et al. (2008) refined the chromosome 2p11.1-q12.2 locus responsible for cortical tremor associated with epilepsy.
quotes: Refinement of the 2p11.1-q12.2 locus responsible for cortical tremor associated with epilepsy

findings.statement: Saint-Martin et al. (2008) excluded candidate genes within the refined 2p11.1-q12.2 locus for cortical tremor associated with epilepsy.
quotes: exclusion of candidate genes

relevance_reason: Clinical description of a large FAME2 family and refinement of the 2q locus.

findings.statement: Crompton et al. (2012) described a 6-generation kindred of European descent with familial adult myoclonic epilepsy, ascertained in New Zealand and Australia. All 55 affected members had fine hand tremor, with onset typically in adolescence (median age 15 years; range 4-60 years). Proximal myoclonus was present in 44 of 55 (80%), arising later than the hand tremor (median 17 years; range 5-60 years), and generalized tonic-clonic seizures occurred in 8 of 55 (15%), with a median age at onset of 43.5 years (range 18-76 years). Neurophysiologic testing confirmed features of cortical reflex myoclonus.
quotes: A 6-generation FAME kindred of European descent was ascertained in New Zealand and Australia. Affected family members (N = 55) had fine hand tremor, with onset typically in adolescence (median age, 15 years; age range, 4-60 years).

Proximal myoclonus was present in 44 of 55 (80%), arising later than hand tremor (median age, 17 years; age range, 5-60 years). Generalized tonic-clonic seizures occurred in 8 of 55 (15%), with a median age at onset of 43.5 years (age range, 18-76 years).
Neurophysiological testing confirmed features of cortical reflex myoclonus.
findings.population: European descent; New Zealand and Australia

findings.statement: Crompton et al. (2012) concluded that the most common FAME phenotype in this large family was mild postural hand tremor resembling essential tremor combined with subtle proximal myoclonus. Generalized tonic-clonic seizures were uncommon and occurred around sleep onset following severe generalized myoclonus.
quotes: The most common FAME phenotype in this large family is mild postural hand tremor resembling essential tremor, combined with subtle proximal myoclonus.
Generalized tonic-clonic seizures are uncommon and occur around sleep onset following severe generalized myoclonus.

phenotypes.text: mild postural hand tremor resembling essential tremor
severe generalized myoclonus preceding seizures at sleep onset

findings.population: European descent; New Zealand and Australia

findings.statement: In the large Australian/New Zealand FAME kindred, Crompton et al. (2012) narrowed the FAME2 locus on chromosome 2 to a 13.3-Mb interval containing 99 known protein-coding genes.
quotes: Genetic mapping narrows the FAME2 (OMIM 607876) locus on chromosome 2 to a 13.3-megabase interval, harboring 99 known protein-coding genes.
findings.population: European descent; New Zealand and Australia

relevance_reason: Reports a new BAFME family with suggestive linkage to the chromosome 2p11.1-q12.2 FAME2 locus, supporting the mapping of FAME2 and genetic heterogeneity.

findings.statement: Striano et al. (2004) described a new family with benign adult familial myoclonic epilepsy (BAFME) and reported suggestive linkage to chromosome 2p11.1-q12.2, with a lod score of 1.55.
quotes: We present a new family with suggestion of linkage to chromosome 2p11.1-2q12.2 (lod score value, 1.55).

findings.statement: Striano et al. (2004) concluded that their observation would confirm that BAFME is a worldwide, genetically heterogeneous condition, probably with Japanese families linked to 8q24 and European families to 2p11.1-q12.2.
quotes: This observation would confirm that BAFME is a worldwide, genetically heterogeneous condition, probably with Japanese families linked to 8q24 and European families to 2p11.1-q12.2.

findings.statement: Striano et al. (2004) described BAFME as an autosomal dominant condition characterized by cortical tremor and generalized seizures.
quotes: Benign adult familial myoclonic epilepsy (BAFME) is an autosomal dominant condition characterized by cortical tremor and generalized seizures

relevance_reason: The paper reports linkage of BAFME to 2p11.1-q12.2, the FAME2 locus, and a shared founder haplotype in five Italian families. It adds mapping and founder evidence but no causative gene.

findings.statement: Madia et al. (2008) genotyped 53 affected individuals from 5 BAFME families from southern Italy, one of them not previously reported. They used microsatellite markers spanning chromosomes 2p11.1-q12.2 and 8q23.1-q24.11. Multipoint linkage analysis found significant linkage to 2p11.1-q12.2, with a maximum cumulative lod score of 18.5 for markers D2S2161 and D2S388.
quotes: DNA from 53 affected individuals was genotyped with highly polymorphic microsatellite markers spanning chromosomes 2p11.1-q12.2 and 8q23.1-q24.11.
Significant linkage was found on chromosome 2p11.1-q12.2 and a maximum cumulative lod score of 18.5 was found for markers D2S2161 and D2S388.

findings.statement: Madia et al. (2008) found that the haplotype '5332' of the adjacent markers D2S388, D2S2216, D2S113, and D2S2175 segregated with the disease in all 5 southern Italian BAFME families. They concluded that these families carry the same mutation inherited from a common ancestor.
quotes: The haplotype "5332" of adjacent markers D2S388, D2S2216, D2S113, and D2S2175 segregates with the disease in all families indicating that the same mutation inherited from a common ancestor segregates in these families.

findings.statement: In a preliminary genotype-phenotype analysis, Madia et al. (2008) found only minor clinical differences among patients carrying the founder disease haplotype. They suggested that other factors do not markedly influence the expressivity of the founder mutation.
quotes: Preliminary genotype-phenotype showed that patients carrying the disease haplotype show minor clinical differences, suggesting that expressivity of the founder mutation is not markedly influenced by other factors.

findings.statement: Madia et al. (2008) described benign adult familial myoclonic epilepsy (BAFME) as an autosomal dominant condition characterized by shivering-like tremors of cortical origin, myoclonus, and epilepsy.
quotes: Benign adult familial myoclonic epilepsy (BAFME or FAME) is an autosomal dominant condition, characterized by shivering-like tremors of cortical origin, myoclonus, and epilepsy.

relevance_reason: Reports two Italian BAFME families linked to chromosome 2p11.1-q12.2, which is the FAME2 locus.

findings.statement: de Falco et al. (2003) reported a clinical and electrophysiologic study of 2 Italian families with benign adult familial myoclonic epilepsy (BAFME). They found linkage to chromosome 2p11.1-q12.2.
quotes: The authors report a clinical and electrophysiologic study of two Italian BAFME families showing linkage to chromosome 2p11.1-q12.2.

findings.statement: de Falco et al. (2003) noted that BAFME had been mapped to chromosome 8q24. Their finding of linkage to 2p11.1-q12.2 in 2 Italian families supported genetic heterogeneity and the existence of non-Japanese families with BAFME. They suggested that this locus might be allelic with the autosomal dominant cortical myoclonus and epilepsy (ADCME) syndrome.
quotes: Benign adult familial myoclonic epilepsy (BAFME) has been mapped to chromosome 8q24; however, genetic heterogeneity has been recently suggested.
Their report supports the evidence of non-Japanese families with BAFME and suggests a possible allelism with the recently described autosomal dominant cortical myoclonus and epilepsy syndrome.

relevance_reason: Reports a large Italian family with cortical tremor, myoclonus and epilepsy linked to chromosome 2p, the FAME2 locus.

findings.statement: Striano et al. (2005) reported a 5-generation family from Naples, Italy, with cortical tremor, myoclonus, and epilepsy. Eleven members, aged 24 to 56 years (mean 39.2 years), had hand tremor and myoclonus, and 6 of them also had generalized seizures. Electrophysiologic study confirmed cortical reflex myoclonus in all affected members.
quotes: We report a five-generation family showing cortical tremor, myoclonus, and epilepsy, originating from Naples, Italy.
Eleven members, aged 24-56 years (mean: 39.2 years), suffered from hand tremor and myoclonus, whereas generalized seizures occurred in six.
Electrophysiological study confirmed the presence of cortical reflex myoclonus in all affected members.

findings.statement: Striano et al. (2005) found giant somatosensory evoked potential components and an enhanced long loop reflex I in 3 presymptomatic members of the family. These members developed hand tremor and upper-limb myoclonus after 1.5 years of follow-up.
quotes: In addition, giant somatosensory-evoked potential components and enhanced long loop reflex I were found also in three presymptomatic members who manifested hand tremor and myoclonus at upper limbs after 1.5 years of follow-up.

findings.statement: In the Italian family with cortical tremor, myoclonus, and epilepsy, Striano et al. (2005) found significant linkage to chromosome 2p, with a maximum lod score of 5.9.
quotes: Genetic study of the pedigree revealed a significant linkage on chromosome 2p (maximum lod score = 5.9).

relevance_reason: Describes a new Italian FCMTE family that does not link to 8q24 and shares a haplotype on pericentromeric chromosome 2, the FAME2 locus.

findings.statement: Suppa et al. (2009) described an Italian family with familial cortical myoclonic tremor with epilepsy (FCMTE). Clinically affected family members had limb and voice tremor, seizures, and myoclonus of the eyelids during blinking. Neuropsychological testing showed visuospatial impairment, which the authors suggested might be due to temporal lobe dysfunction. Neurophysiologic findings suggested increased excitability of the primary motor cortex with normal sensorimotor integration.
quotes: Clinically affected members of the family had limb and voice tremor, seizures, and myoclonus involving the eyelids during blinking.
Neuropsychological testing disclosed visuospatial impairment, possibly due to temporal lobe dysfunction.
Neurophysiologic findings suggested increased primary motor cortex excitability with normal sensorimotor integration.

findings.statement: In the Italian FCMTE family, Suppa et al. (2009) excluded linkage to the 8q24 locus. Affected members shared a common haplotype spanning 14.5 Mb in the pericentromeric region of chromosome 2.
quotes: Linkage analysis excluded the 8q24 locus, where patients shared a common haplotype spanning 14.5 Mb in the pericentromeric region of chromosome 2.

findings.statement: Suppa et al. (2009) excluded the 8q24 locus by linkage analysis in an Italian FCMTE family. This is evidence of genetic heterogeneity, with the family instead sharing a haplotype on pericentromeric chromosome 2.
quotes: Linkage analysis excluded the 8q24 locus, where patients shared a common haplotype spanning 14.5 Mb in the pericentromeric region of chromosome 2.

relevance_reason: Uses identity-by-descent mapping to narrow the FAME2 locus at 2p11.2-q11.2 and gives evidence of an Italian founder effect and allelic heterogeneity at this locus.

findings.statement: Henden et al. (2016) performed identity-by-descent (IBD) analysis on high-density SNP array data from a FAME cohort of 10 European families and 1 Australian/New Zealander family, 8 of which had known disease loci. By finding IBD regions shared by several families, they narrowed the FAME2 locus to a 9.78-Mb interval within 2p11.2-q11.2. They also suggested candidate disease genes by prioritizing genes with gene co-expression analysis.
quotes: We performed an IBD analysis using high-density single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) array data followed by gene prioritization on a FAME cohort of ten European families and one Australian/New Zealander family; eight of which had known disease loci.
By identifying IBD regions common to multiple families, we were able to narrow the FAME2 locus to a 9.78 megabase interval within 2p11.2-q11.2.

findings.statement: Henden et al. (2016) gave additional evidence of a founder effect in 4 Italian families with FAME2. They also found allelic heterogeneity at the FAME2 locus, with at least 4 distinct founders responsible for the disease.
quotes: We provide additional evidence of a founder effect in four Italian families and allelic heterogeneity with at least four distinct founders responsible for FAME at the FAME2 locus.

findings.statement: Henden et al. (2016) described familial adult myoclonus epilepsy (FAME) as a rare autosomal dominant disorder. It is characterized by adult onset, involuntary muscle jerks, cortical myoclonus and occasional seizures. They noted that FAME is genetically heterogeneous, with more than 70 families reported worldwide and 5 potential disease loci.
quotes: Familial adult myoclonus epilepsy (FAME) is a rare autosomal dominant disorder characterized by adult onset, involuntary muscle jerks, cortical myoclonus and occasional seizures.
FAME is genetically heterogeneous with more than 70 families reported worldwide and five potential disease loci.

relevance_reason: Describes a new large Italian FCMTE family that links to the FCMTE2 locus on 2p11.1-q12.2. It narrows the critical interval and confirms a founder haplotype. No gene was identified.

findings.statement: Licchetta et al. (2013) described a large family with familial cortical myoclonic tremor and epilepsy (FCMTE). Of the 127 family members, 25 were affected (9 males, 16 females), and 16 of the 19 living affected members were studied (mean age 47.8 years). Cortical myoclonic tremor was associated with generalized seizures in 10 patients (62.5%). Mean age at onset was 28.1 years for cortical myoclonic tremor and 33.8 years for seizures. Four patients (25%) reported slow progression of the tremor, with severe gait impairment in 1, and psychiatric disorders of variable severity occurred in 37.5% of cases.
quotes: The pedigree included 25 affected members (M/F: 9/16). We studied 16 of the 19 living affected members (M/F: 5/11; mean age 47.8 years). Cortical myoclonic tremor (CMT) was associated with generalized seizures in 10 patients (62.5%).
The mean age at onset of CMT and seizures was 28.1 and 33.8 years, respectively. Four patients (25%) reported a slow progression of CMT, with severe gait impairment in one.
Psychiatric disorders of variable severity recurred in 37.5% of cases.

findings.statement: Licchetta et al. (2013) performed polygraphic studies in 15 family members and back-averaging and somatosensory evoked potentials with C-reflex studies in 4. Rhythmic bursts at 7 to 15 Hz were recorded in all 11 affected members tested, and the additional studies showed a cortical origin of myoclonus in all patients tested. Generalized epileptiform discharges were recorded in 25% of cases and a photoparoxysmal response in 31%.
quotes: Rhythmic bursts at 7-15 Hz were recorded in all 11 affected members tested. Additional neurophysiologic investigations disclosed a cortical origin of myoclonus in all patients tested.
Generalized epileptiform discharges were recorded in 25% of cases, and a photoparoxysmal response in 31%.

findings.statement: Licchetta et al. (2013) genotyped 30 family members with microsatellite markers at the FCMTE1 (8q), FCMTE2 (2p), and FCMTE3 (5p) loci. They established linkage to the FCMTE2 locus on chromosome 2p11.1-q12.2 and narrowed the critical interval to a 10.4-Mb segment. This reduced the number of positional candidate genes to 59.
quotes: The genetic study investigated 30 subjects with microsatellite markers at three loci on chromosomes 8q (FCMTE1), 2p (FCMTE2), and 5p (FCMTE3).
Genetic analysis established linkage to the FCMTE2 locus on chromosome 2p11.1-2q12.2 (OMIM 607876) and narrowed the critical interval to a 10.4 Mb segment.
reduces the number of positional candidate genes in the FCMTE2 locus to 59

findings.statement: Licchetta et al. (2013) found that the family carried a founder haplotype identical to the one previously seen in FCMTE2 families from the same geographic area. They concluded that this confirms a founder effect in Italian families.
quotes: Haplotype analysis in the present family identified a founder haplotype identical to that previously observed in families from the same geographic area.
This study confirms evidence of a founder effect in Italian families
